textbookText: Figure 8.3.1 Pheretima posthuma (a) Ventral view (b) dorsal view of anterior end of body 4. Clitellum or Cingulum There is a prominent, thick and circular band of glandular tissue in mature worm surrounding 14th, 15th and 16th segment which is called clitellum or cingulum. Clitellum consists of albumen secreting cells, mucous secreting cells and cocoon forming cells. Clitellum divides the body into: pre-clitellar region (from the 1st to the 13th segment), cliteller region (from the 14th to the 16th segment) and post-clitellar region (from the 17th up to the last segment). 5. Setae All segments except first, last and clitellar segments bear a ring of chitionous and backwardly directed bristles called setae. Setae are found embedded in the body wall, arranged in the row at the middle of each segment. Their number ranges from 80-120 per segment and arrangement is called perichaetine. A seta has a light-yellow colour, and shape like elongated ‘S’ with a swollen middle part called nodulus. Locomotion takes place in earthworm with the help of setae. Movement of setae is controlled by some special muscles called protractor and retractor muscles of the body wall.

Figure 8.3.2 T.S of body wall through setae 6. External apertures or openings There are several openings or apertures on the body wall of earthworm which are listed below: i. Mouth: It is a crescent shaped and anterior most opening situated in the first segment called peristomium. It is ventrally located.

Figure 8.3.3 location of mouth ii. Spermathecal pores: There are altogether four pairs of small apertures of spermathecae (sperm storing sacs) and each pair situated at the intersegmental groove of 5th and 6th, 6th and 7th, 7th and 8th, 8th and 9th in ventro-lateral position. iii. Nephridiopores: A large number of very minute openings of integumentary nephridia are found scattered throughout the body of earthworm except first two segments. These openings are used for the removal of metabolic nitrogenous wastes extracted from blood capillaries. iv. Dorsal pores: These minute apertures are found along the mid -dorsal line in the intersegmental groove from 12th and 13th segment onwards except the last groove. They are the opening of coelomic chambers through which coelomic fluid oozes, making body moist.
Figure 8.3.4 location dorsal pores Biology, Grade 11 | 359

v. Female genital aperture: A single median aperture or opening of common oviduct lying on the ventral surface of 14th segment called female genital opening which is used for discharging out ova. vi. Male genital apertures: There is a pair of crescentic openings situated on the ventrolateral surface of 18th segment which are called as male genital openings. They are used to discharge sperms during copulation by earthworms. vii. Anus: It is a vertical slit like opening at the posterior most segment of the body called pygidium or anal segment. It is the last part of alimentary canal through which faecal matters are discharged.

7. Genital papillae Genital papillae are two pairs in number and structurally; they are prominent rounded elevations, each pair in the 17th and 19th segment; each in ventro-lateral position. These papillae are used for the attachment of two mature worms during copulation.

Figure 8.3.5 apertures in 13th to 19th segments magnified Body wall of Earthworm Body wall of earthworm is thin, soft, elastic and moist which is composed of four layers. These layers are cuticle, epidermis, a well-developed muscular layer and a thin parietal layer of coelomic epithelium from outside. 1. Cuticle: Cuticle is a thin, elastic, non-living and finely striated layer which forms the external protective covering of the body. It is composed of two layer of collagen fibres mixed with a polysaccharide and small amount of gelatin. It is secreted by underlying epidermis. Cuticle also consists of numerous pores through which epidermal glands and nephridia open out.

Figure 8.3.6 T.S of body wall of earthworm 2. Epidermis: This is a single layer of epithelial cells lying just below cuticle resting on basement membrane. The constituent cells are of different types: supporting cells, gland cells, basal cells, sensory receptor cells.
• Supporting cells form the major bulk of epidermis and secrete cuticle. • Gland cells comprise mucous cell and albumen cell which secrete mucus and albumen
